papers.title: Cenobamate in brain tumor-related epilepsy: A multicenter real-world experience.
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Cenobamate (CNB) is a novel antiseizure medication with a dual mechanism of action that has demonstrated high efficacy in drug-resistant focal epilepsy; however, evidence in brain tumor-related epilepsy (BTRE) remains limited. The study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness, safety, and tolerability of CNB as add-on therapy in a multicenter cohort of patients with BTRE.
METHODS: We conducted a multicenter, retrospective observational study across tertiary epilepsy centers in the Lazio region, Italy. Adult patients with drug-resistant BTRE treated with CNB as adjunctive therapy were included. Seizure frequency was assessed at baseline and during follow-up. Primary outcomes were changes in monthly seizure frequency and responder rates. Effectiveness was analyzed in both the overall population and in a homogeneous cohort of patients with 6-month follow-up.
RESULTS: Twenty patients (10 females, median age 48 years) were included. Tumor histology included meningioma (n = 7, 35%), astrocytoma (n = 4, 20%), glioblastoma (n = 3, 15%), ganglioglioma (n = 3, 15%), oligodendroglioma (n = 2, 10%), and dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor (n = 1, 5%). In the overall analysis population (n = 20), after a median 12-month follow-up, median seizure frequency significantly decreased from 6 to 1 per month (p < 0.001), with a median reduction of 85.8% (IQR 51.4-96.7). Responder rates were 80% (≥50% seizure reduction), 60% (≥75%), and 20% achieved seizure freedom. Adverse events occurred in 12 patients (60%), including sedation (n = 8, 40%), postural instability (n = 3, 15%), diarrhea, and mild cutaneous rash (n = 1, 5% each). CNB was discontinued in one patient (5%).
SIGNIFICANCE: In this multicenter real-world cohort of patients with drug-resistant BTRE and heterogeneous tumor histology, CNB was associated with a reduction in seizure frequency and was well tolerated.
PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: Seizures caused by brain tumors can be difficult to control. We reviewed records from 20 adults who received cenobamate alongside their existing seizure medicines. At their last follow-up, 16 had at least half as many seizures, and four were seizure-free. Twelve patients experienced side effects, most commonly sleepiness; one stopped cenobamate because of a rash. These findings suggest that cenobamate may help some people with brain tumor-related epilepsy. However, the study was small, had no comparison group, and included patients with different tumors and follow-up durations. Larger studies are needed.

papers.title: Invasive monitoring and mapping in epilepsy surgery: Acute and chronic intracranial recording from surface to depth.
papers.journal: Epileptic disorders : international epilepsy journal with videotape
papers.abstract: Invasive intracranial recording remains central to the surgical evaluation of drug-resistant focal epilepsy when noninvasive data are insufficient to define the epileptogenic zone or its relationship to eloquent cortex. This review, part of an International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) Surgical Therapies Commission education series aligned with the epilepsy surgery curriculum, reviews invasive monitoring and mapping for the practicing and trainee epilepsy surgeon. Consistent with the competency-based ILAE epilepsy surgery curriculum, in which the surgeon is expected to understand and actively contribute to electrode selection, safe implantation, and the interpretation of invasive recordings within the multidisciplinary team, we give particular emphasis to the surgical execution of these methods alongside their electrophysiological rationale. We outline the historical development of the field from intraoperative electrocorticography and subdural recording to stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG), describe acute and chronic recording strategies using both surface and depth approaches, including the operative techniques of implantation and post-implantation electrode localization, and summarize the techniques of functional mapping. We compare subdural and stereotactic methods with respect to coverage, mapping capability, diagnostic yield, seizure outcome, and morbidity, and we review the complication profiles of each. Finally, we discuss future directions, including high-density and chronically implantable probes that combine macro-contacts with microelectrode recording throughout the electrode shaft. We emphasize that the choice of method should follow a clearly stated anatomo-electro-clinical hypothesis, balancing the completeness of sampling against procedural risk.

papers.title: Laser interstitial thermal therapy in older patients with drug-resistant mesial temporal lobe epilepsy.
papers.journal: Epileptic disorders : international epilepsy journal with videotape
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT) is a minimally invasive treatment for focal drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE). This study sought to examine the efficacy of LITT for a cohort of older adults with mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE) and evaluate predictors of safety.
METHODS: We examined 24 patients aged ≥50 years, with 10/24 (42%) ≥60 years. Primary outcomes were Engel classification and reduction from baseline seizure frequency. We additionally reviewed post-ablation complications, hospital length of stay (LOS), neurocognitive and psychiatric worsening, and anti-seizure medication (ASM) reduction. The Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) was calculated to assess its utility in prediction of postoperative complications.
RESULTS: 22/24 (92%) had ≥50% reduction in seizure frequency, and 17/24 (71%) had ≥90% reduction at last follow-up, with median follow-up of 5.2 years (range, 1.5-10.4 years). Engel Class I outcome was achieved in 19/24 (79%) of patients by 6 months post-ablation and maintained in 12/24 (50%) of patients by last follow-up. Immediate postoperative complications were mostly transient, though worse cognitive symptoms were reported in 5/24 (21%), and worse mood was reported in 3/24 (13%) at 6 months post-ablation. Higher CCI did not correlate with complications but was associated with prolonged LOS. ASM reduction occurred in half of patients.
SIGNIFICANCE: In our cohort, LITT offered favorable seizure and safety outcomes in an older population with focal DRE. Perioperative risk assessments such as the CCI may be useful in older patient selection for LITT.

papers.title: Preoperative hippocampal volume, resection extent, and 5-year stability of seizure freedom after temporal lobe epilepsy surgery.
papers.journal: Epileptic disorders : international epilepsy journal with videotape
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To examine whether preoperative ipsilateral hippocampal volume modifies the association between hippocampal resection extent and durable 5-year seizure freedom after temporal lobe epilepsy surgery.
METHODS: We performed a retrospective secondary analysis of the public Imaging Database for Epilepsy And Surgery. Patients undergoing temporal lobectomy or temporal lesionectomy were eligible. The exposure was ipsilateral hippocampal resection fraction, the modifier was preoperative ipsilateral hippocampal volume z-score, and the outcome was International League Against Epilepsy class 1 at every annual assessment from years 1 through 5. Multivariable logistic regression included their interaction and pathology, procedure type, preoperative focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizures, age, epilepsy duration, antiseizure medication count, sex, and operative side.
RESULTS: Among 353 patients undergoing temporal surgery, 220 had all five annual outcomes and 210 had complete primary-model data. Durable seizure freedom occurred in 82 of 210 patients (39.0%). The resection-by-volume interaction odds ratio was 1.49 (95% confidence interval, 1.01-2.21; p = .045). Model-based probabilities increased with greater resection when hippocampal volume was preserved but not with marked atrophy. The estimate was similar in temporal lobectomy alone (odds ratio, 1.74; 95% confidence interval, 1.07-2.83) and attenuated after inverse-probability weighting (odds ratio, 1.43; 95% confidence interval, .95-2.13).
SIGNIFICANCE: In this cohort, the association between measured hippocampal resection overlap and seizure outcome varied across preoperative hippocampal volumes. The pattern was most apparent when seizure freedom was assessed across 5 years rather than at a single postoperative visit.

papers.title: Extracellular vesicles enable rotavirus and astrovirus infection of low-susceptibility cell lines.
papers.abstract: Rotaviruses (RVA) and human astroviruses (HAstV) are classical gastrointestinal pathogens, but increasing evidence indicates that they are also involved in a range of extraintestinal diseases. These include seizures and diabetes in RVA infections, and central nervous system infections in HAstV infections. However, the mechanisms by which these viruses disseminate beyond the intestine remain unclear. Given the previously described association of RVA and HAstV with extracellular vesicles (EVs), we investigated whether purified EV-virus complexes could mediate infection of cells with low susceptibility to these viruses. We found that the RVA strain RRV, as well as two HAstV strains (the classical HAstV-8, Yuc8 strain, and the divergent non-classical VA1 strain), could infect low-susceptibility cell lines (BHK, SK-N-SH, F11, and CHO) when associated with EVs. This infectivity was dependent on EV integrity, since disruption of vesicles by detergent treatment reduced infection. Furthermore, a fraction of viral particles was protected from neutralizing antibodies, most likely because they were enclosed within EVs. Together, these findings suggest that EVs may act as vehicles facilitating the dissemination of RVA and HAstV beyond the gastrointestinal tract.IMPORTANCEGastrointestinal viruses typically infect specific intestinal cell types; however, rotaviruses (RVA) and human astroviruses (HAstV) have been associated with a range of extraintestinal pathologies. To better understand how these viruses disseminate beyond the intestine, we investigated the potential role of their interactions with extracellular vesicles (EVs). We found that the simian RVA strain RRV and HAstV strains Yuc8 and VA1, when associated with EVs, could infect low-susceptibility cells. A fraction of the EV-associated viral particles was resistant to antibody-mediated neutralization, suggesting that EVs protected them. These observations support the possibility that EVs could serve as vehicles enabling RVA and HAstV to disseminate beyond the gastrointestinal tract.

papers.title: Prospective genotype-guided drug selection and dosing in alcohol withdrawal syndrome complicated by seizures: a randomized clinical trial.
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To determine whether prospective genotype-guided drug selection and dosing can reduce cumulative withdrawal severity and improve treatment tolerability in alcohol withdrawal syndrome (AWS) complicated by seizures.
METHODS: In this single-center, parallel-group randomized clinical trial, 100 inpatients with AWS and seizures were allocated 1:1 to a genotype-guided prescribing strategy or control. All patients were genotyped on admission for CYP2D6*4, CYP2C19*2, CYP2C19*17, CYP3A4*1B, CYP3A5*3, and ABCB1 3435C>T. Intervention-group physicians received an individualized report with recommendations on benzodiazepine and anticonvulsant selection and starting dose; control-group physicians received a format-matched report without individualized recommendations. The primary outcome was area under the CIWA-Ar curve over 0-72 h, assessed by a blinded rater.
RESULTS: AUC CIWA-Ar was 774.3 ± 175.9 vs. 903.6 ± 199.5 score-hours (mean difference -129.3; 95 % CI -204.0 to -54.6; p<0.001). Confirmed stabilization by 48 h occurred in 31/50 vs. 20/50 patients (log-rank p=0.020; Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted p=0.051, not significant after multiplicity correction). UKU side-effect scores were lower on days 3 and 5 (both p<0.001), and excessive sedation occurred in 1/50 vs. 9/50 patients (p=0.016). Total benzodiazepine load was lower with genotype guidance (25.0 vs. 27.5 mg diazepam equivalents; p=0.016). The composite rate of clinically significant adverse events and the rates of delirium and unplanned treatment modification did not differ significantly.
CONCLUSIONS: A prospective genotype-informed prescribing strategy was associated with lower cumulative withdrawal severity and less excessive sedation while using a lower benzodiazepine load. Because the intervention also changed anticonvulsant selection and drug concentrations were not measured, these findings support the clinical strategy as a whole rather than any single genotype-to-dose rule. Multicenter, prospectively registered trials with measured drug exposure are warranted.

papers.title: First Seizure Services: Status and Healthcare Professional Attitudes and Perspectives. Results From a Survey of the European Academy of Neurology.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Dedicated first seizure services (FSSs) may improve the early assessment, diagnosis, and management of people presenting with a suspected first seizure, but little is known regarding their current status in Europe. In this study, we aimed to explore the availability of FSSs throughout Europe, as well as to investigate attitudes towards their implementation among healthcare professionals involved in epilepsy care.
METHODS: We designed a web-based survey that was distributed through the European Academy of Neurology. The survey assessed respondent characteristics, local FSS availability, service organization, perceived utility, and barriers to implementation.
RESULTS: A total of 441 participants from 72 countries completed the survey; 379 unique centers were included in center-specific analyses. Overall, 171/331 centers in geographical Europe (51.7%) reported an available FSS. Availability varied significantly by region, being highest in Northern Europe (74.0%) and lowest in Eastern Europe (35.5%). FSS availability correlated positively with Gross Domestic Product and current health expenditure per capita of the respondent's country. Participants reported a positive attitude towards FSSs: 90.9% believed that they should be a standard of care, 93.2% believed they improve outcomes, and 83.0% believed that they are cost-effective. The main reported barriers to implementation were limited infrastructure, financial constraints, organizational barriers, and a shortage of specialized personnel.
CONCLUSIONS: FSS availability across Europe remains heterogeneous, with substantial variation according to geographical area and a possible association with economic factors. Despite implementation barriers, healthcare professionals expressed overall positive support for standardized first seizure pathways.

papers.title: Blood Pressure Variability in Brain Arteriovenous Malformations: a Review of Pathophysiological Mechanisms, Clinical Relevance, and Therapeutic Insights.
papers.abstract: Brain arteriovenous malformations (bAVMs) are high-flow vascular lesions linked to substantial hemorrhage risk and neurological impairment. Traditional risk stratification centers on static hemodynamic parameters, but blood pressure variability (BPV)-fluctuations in blood pressure over time-has emerged as a dynamic, modifiable risk factor. This review explores how pathophysiological pathways link BPV to bAVMs progression and rupture, with specific focus on how aberrant hemodynamics, endothelial dysfunction, compromised cerebral autoregulation, and blood steal syndrome interact. We look at how BPV can worsen wall stress, spark inflammatory responses, and drive vascular restructuring-all of which raise rupture risk. We discuss BPV's clinical impacts in both unruptured and ruptured bAVMs, including how it affects perioperative outcomes and long-term functional recovery. We also assess BPV as a therapeutic target, highlighting pharmacological and monitoring strategies built to stabilize blood pressure fluctuations. Finally, we point out critical knowledge gaps and suggest future research directions to fold BPV into personalized risk assessment and management protocols for bAVMs.

papers.title: Adult phenotype of genetically confirmed Dravet syndrome: diagnostic challenges and clinical red flags from a multicenter Polish cohort.
papers.abstract:
AIM OF THE STUDY: To characterize the clinical phenotype of adults with clinically diagnosed and genetically confirmed Dravet syndrome (DS), with particular emphasis on seizure evolution, cognitive and motor impairment, and diagnostic delay.
CLINICAL RATIONALE FOR THE STUDY: An increasing number of individuals with DS survive into adulthood and require long-term neurological care. However, the adult phenotype differs from the classical childhood presentation and remains underrecognized in adult neurological practice. Recognition of an age-evolving seizure phenotype, together with intellectual disability, gait and postural abnormalities, and extrapyramidal features, may provide important diagnostic clues and prompt molecular testing in previously undiagnosed adults.
MATERIAL AND METHODS: We conducted a multicenter retrospective case series of nine adults (six females and three males) fulfilling clinical diagnostic criteria for DS and carrying a pathogenic or likely pathogenic SCN1A variant. Clinical data were obtained from medical records, neurological examinations, seizure diaries, and psychological assessments performed as part of routine care. Seizure history and evolution, status epilepticus, cognitive and communication impairment, motor phenotype, and treatment history were analyzed.
RESULTS: The mean age at evaluation was 27.8 years (range 21-37 years). Seizure onset occurred at a mean age of 6 months, whereas the mean age at molecular diagnosis was 13.2 years, corresponding to a mean diagnostic delay of 12.7 years. Febrile seizures occurred in eight of nine patients and persisted beyond the age of 18 years in three. Generalized tonic-clonic seizures persisted into adulthood in all patients, whereas status epilepticus occurred after the age of 18 years in only one. Intellectual disability was present in all patients and was severe or profound in six; communication impairment was observed in eight. Motor abnormalities were prominent, including gait impairment (9/9), ataxia (8/9), postural abnormalities (8/9), bradykinesia (5/9), hypomimia (5/9), and parkinsonian features (3/9). All patients had been exposed to sodium channel-blocking antiseizure medications before molecular diagnosis, with seizure worsening documented in eight of nine patients.
CONCLUSIONS AND CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS: The adult phenotype of DS combines persistent drug-resistant epilepsy with intellectual and communication impairment and prominent motor dysfunction. Although generalized tonic-clonic seizures may persist, other features of the epileptic phenotype, particularly status epilepticus, become less prominent with age. Gait, postural, cerebellar, and extrapyramidal abnormalities may provide important diagnostic clues in adults with infantile-onset epilepsy and intellectual disability. Recognition of this age-evolving phenotype may facilitate molecular diagnosis and support syndrome-specific management in adult neurological practice.

papers.title: [Comparison of prehospital management of selected emergencies between a paramedical team and a physician-led team : a retrospective study in Belgium].
papers.abstract: In Belgium, the emergency medical system (EMS) coordinates mobile emergency and resuscitation units (SMUR) and paramedical intervention teams (PIT). As demand increases, greater use of PITs could help relieve SMUR workload, although comparative data remain limited. This retrospective study compared prehospital care by analysing 2,325 prehospital interventions (PIT = 1,377; SMUR = 948) involving cardiac arrest, trauma, seizures, chest pain, and acute respiratory disorders. Patient characteristics, response times, and management strategies were analysing. Management of cardiac arrest and seizures was comparable between the two intervention systems. In trauma cases, both patient characteristics and therapeutic interventions differed. In patients with chest pain, SMUR teams performed more electrocardiograms. For respiratory conditions, PIT teams more frequently administered oxygen therapy and aerosol treatment, whereas SMUR teams more often performed intubation. No difference was observed in response times. Overall, PIT appears to be a useful alternative when SMUR is unavailable; however, prospective studies are needed before confirming comparable performance between the two systems.

papers.title: 18F-FDG PET/MR Findings in Sturge-Weber Syndrome During Presurgical Evaluation of Drug-Resistant Epilepsy.
papers.abstract: 18F-FDG PET/MR demonstrated extensive right cerebral cortical hypometabolism in a 52-year-old man with Sturge-Weber syndrome undergoing presurgical evaluation of drug-resistant epilepsy. Clinical photographs showed capillary malformations involving the face and both hands. CT revealed prominent right hemispheric gyriform calcifications, while integrated 18F-FDG PET/MR demonstrated ipsilateral cerebral atrophy and reduced cortical uptake in the frontoparietal and temporal lobes. These images illustrate the complementary roles of CT and 18F-FDG PET/MR in characterizing structural abnormalities and regional metabolic impairment in longstanding Sturge-Weber syndrome.

papers.title: Hidden in Plain Sight: An Unusual Case of Neurocysticercosis.
papers.abstract: Neurocysticercosis (NCC), caused by the larval stage of Taenia solium, is a leading cause of acquired epilepsy in endemic regions and is increasingly encountered in non-endemic countries due to migration and travel [1,4]. NCC results from fecal-oral ingestion of T. solium eggs from a human tapeworm carrier rather than from pork consumption [4]. Intraventricular NCC may present without seizures and can mimic primary headache syndromes or cranial neuralgias while causing obstructive hydrocephalus [1,2]. We report a 68-year-old woman with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, prior right V1 herpes zoster, and a reported cerebrovascular event who presented with years of severe right-sided headache and shooting facial pain (V1-V3). Initial diagnoses favored zoster-related neuralgia, and neuropathic medications provided minimal relief. Brain MRI revealed a predominantly cystic, non-enhancing lesion filling the fourth ventricle with ventriculomegaly consistent with chronic obstructive hydrocephalus. Progressive ventricular enlargement prompted neurosurgical intervention. Suboccipital craniotomy with cyst excision and external ventricular drain placement was performed. Pathology demonstrated calcified cysticercus structures, confirming NCC, and serum cysticercus IgG was positive. The patient was treated with albendazole and corticosteroids, with improvement in headache. Fourth ventricular NCC may masquerade as chronic unilateral headache or trigeminal neuralgia, and progressive ventriculomegaly should prompt consideration of intraventricular NCC in at-risk patients. Early recognition is essential to prevent decompensated hydrocephalus and guide appropriate neurosurgical and antiparasitic management [1,3].

papers.title: A Homozygous SLC39A8 p.Asn369Thr Variant in an Infant With Leigh-Like Encephalopathy.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Biallelic variants of SLC39A8 cause congenital disorders of glycosylation Type IIn (CDG-IIn, OMIM #616721), a rare autosomal recessive condition characterized by impaired manganese (Mn) transport, defective glycosylation, and secondary mitochondrial dysfunction. Affected infants present with developmental delays, hypotonia, seizures, and symmetric basal ganglia lesions on brain MRI.
CASE PRESENTATION: An 11-month-old girl, previously developmentally appropriate, presented with new-onset seizures and regression of motor and social milestones. Examination revealed global hypotonia, poor feeding, and faltered growth. Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral, symmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintensities with restricted diffusion in the caudate nuclei, putamin, globi pallidi, subthalamic nuclei, and cerebral peduncles, with sparing of the dentate nuclei and no contrast enhancement. Whole exome sequencing identified a novel homozygous SLC39A8 variant, NM_001,135,146.2:c.1106A > C (p.Asn369Thr). Each parent was a heterozygous carrier, confirming autosomal recessive inheritance. This variant is absent from ClinVar and gnomAD and is currently classified as a variant of uncertain significance (VUS). The clinical phenotype and neuroimaging pattern are compatible with SLC39A8-CDG; however, the identified variant remains a VUS, and biochemical confirmation could not be obtained because the relevant tests were unavailable. Confirmation would require functional studies. Supportive testing would include transferrin glycosylation analysis and blood manganese measurement; a normal conventional transferrin result alone would not exclude the diagnosis. If SLC39A8-CDG is confirmed, manganese and galactose supplementation should be considered only under specialist metabolic supervision with appropriate biochemical monitoring. This case suggests a possible phenotype-genotype association but does not establish the pathogenicity of p.Asn369Thr.

papers.title: Exertional syncope caused by acquired obstruction of the pulmonary artery due to an organized thrombus in a dog.
papers.abstract: An 8.5-year-old Boxer was referred for evaluation of frequently occurring exercise-induced seizure-like episodes for 2.5 months. Cardiac auscultation revealed a left basilar systolic murmur with an intensity of IV/VI. Echocardiography showed severe pulmonary arterial obstruction with a pressure gradient of 90 mmHg due to a suspected intraluminal mass. Cardiac catheterization was performed, where a right ventriculogram revealed a large rounded filling defect in the pulmonary artery trunk. No balloon angioplasty, biopsy or stenting were attempted. After euthanasia, post-mortem examination revealed an organized thrombus of unknown etiology attached to the wall of the pulmonary artery trunk. The adjacent arterial wall showed a markedly thickened intimal layer. The etiology remains unclear, primarily due to the chronic nature of the condition. Antemortem blood tests and postmortem examination failed to reveal any prothrombotic conditions. Acquired causes of pulmonary arterial obstruction are extremely rare in dogs, and an organized thrombus has not been reported yet.

papers.title: From Prevalence to Prediction: A Cross-Sectional Study to Develop a Novel Risk Score for Hearing Loss in High-Risk Neonates in South India.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIM: Neonates admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) with multiple risk factors are more likely to develop hearing loss. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of hearing loss, identify its predictive factors, and develop a novel clinical risk score for hearing loss among high-risk neonates.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This cross-sectional study included 105 high-risk neonates admitted to the NICU from July 2024 to June 2025. The hearing assessment protocol included transient-evoked otoacoustic emissions at discharge and at six weeks of corrected age, followed by diagnostic brainstem-evoked response audiometry at three months. Associations between risk factors and hearing loss were analyzed using logistic regression. A novel clinical risk score was developed using the factors significantly associated with hearing loss.
RESULTS: The prevalence of hearing loss among high-risk neonates was 4.8% (95% CI, 1.6%-10.8%). Hearing loss was significantly associated with intrauterine toxoplasmosis, perinatal asphyxia, neonatal hyperbilirubinemia (NNH) requiring exchange transfusion, stage II or higher hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, neonatal sepsis, neonatal seizures, syndromic or craniofacial anomalies, and ototoxic drug exposure (p < 0.05). The clinical risk prediction model, developed using significant predictive factors and assigning double weight to intrauterine toxoplasmosis and NNH requiring exchange transfusion, achieved a sensitivity of 60% and a specificity of 96% at a cutoff score of ≥3.
CONCLUSIONS: The prevalence of hearing loss among high-risk neonates was 4.8%. The novel clinical risk score developed in this study may help guide targeted screening, timely diagnosis, and early intervention for hearing loss.

papers.title: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome Presenting as Late Postpartum Eclampsia in a Previously Normotensive Woman: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) is a clinico-radiological syndrome characterized by acute neurological manifestations, including headache and seizures, with neuroimaging evidence of predominantly reversible vasogenic cerebral edema. It is commonly associated with hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, particularly preeclampsia and eclampsia. A 27-year-old primigravida with known Hashimoto thyroiditis, treated with levothyroxine 50 µg daily, presented on postpartum day seven with a severe headache followed by two generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Her blood pressure was 160/110 mmHg, and the urine protein-to-creatinine ratio was 6.96 g/g creatinine. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain demonstrated bilateral parieto-occipital cortical and subcortical T2-weighted/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintensities consistent with PRES. Magnetic resonance venography excluded cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. Autoimmune investigations for alternative systemic autoimmune disorders, including antinuclear antibody, anti-double-stranded DNA antibody, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, and complement levels, were unremarkable. She was treated with magnesium sulfate and antihypertensive therapy, resulting in complete clinical recovery and resolution of the radiological abnormalities. This case highlights late postpartum eclampsia presenting as PRES in a previously normotensive woman and emphasizes the importance of maintaining a high index of suspicion for postpartum hypertensive disorders in women presenting with new-onset headache or seizures, even after an apparently uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. Early recognition and prompt treatment are essential to prevent potentially life-threatening complications and achieve favorable clinical outcomes.

papers.title: A Novel DHX9 Variant Was Identified in a Patient With Developmental Delay, Facial Dysmorphism and Seizure.
papers.journal: International journal of developmental neuroscience : the official journal of the International Society for Developmental Neuroscience
papers.abstract: The DHX9 gene encodes an RNA helicase belonging to the DExD/H-box family, which is highly expressed in the brain and nervous system. Pathogenic variants in the DHX9 gene are associated with neurodevelopmental disorder (NDD) and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMT). Both loss-of-function (LoF) and missense variants can cause NDD, whereas CMT is associated with specific missense variants. Patients with DHX9-related NDD typically present with intellectual disability, language and motor developmental delay, and autism spectrum disorder (ASD). CMT patients primarily present with distal weakness, sensory deficits, variable muscle wasting, foot deformities and painful sensory neuropathy. Here, we report a female patient with severe DHX9-related NDD phenotypes, including global developmental delay, ASD, facial dysmorphism, epilepsy, microcephaly, abnormal brain MRI findings and clinodactyly of the fifth finger. She experienced her first febrile seizure at 1 year and 2 months of age. She developed frequent myoclonic seizures characterized by rapid nodding and upper body tremors lasting 3-10 s at the age of 3 years. Simultaneous electroencephalogram (EEG) revealed paroxysmal bursts of high- to very-high-amplitude sharp-slow waves, spike-slow waves and polyspike-wave complexes diffusely over bilateral leads. Clinical exome sequencing (CES) identified a likely de novo missense variant in the DHX9 gene in the patient (NM_001357.5, c.1540C>T, p.(His514Tyr)). Notably, this variant resides within the highly conserved DEIH motif (Motif II) of the helicase ATP-binding domain. This critical region plays an essential role in ATP hydrolysis and helicase function. Three-dimensional protein structure modelling suggested that the p.(His514Tyr) substitution may compromise local protein stability by altering hydrogen bond networks. Our study expands the genetic and phenotypic spectrum of DHX9 variant-associated disorders.

papers.title: Optimal Timing of Cranioplasty Following Decompressive Craniectomy: An 8-Year Retrospective Single-Center Analysis of 184 Patients.
papers.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Decompressive craniectomy (DC) is an established life-saving procedure for patients with refractory intracranial hypertension. After stabilization, cranioplasty (CP) is performed to restore cranial integrity, improve cerebral hemodynamics, and protect the brain. However, CP is associated with considerable complication rates, and the optimal timing of reconstruction remains controversial.
AIM: To evaluate the impact of cranioplasty timing on postoperative complications and functional outcomes following decompressive craniectomy, and to identify independent predictors of adverse events after reconstruction.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: We conducted a retrospective single-center cohort study including 184 adult patients who underwent cranioplasty after decompressive craniectomy between January 2017 and December 2024. Patients were categorized according to the interval between DC and CP into early (≤3 months), intermediate (3-6 months), and delayed (>6 months) groups. Demographic, clinical, and surgical variables were analyzed, including age, sex, indication for DC, Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), cranial defect size, implant material, and ventriculoperitoneal shunt dependency. The primary outcome was the occurrence of postoperative complications. Secondary outcomes included surgical site infection, postoperative hematoma, hydrocephalus requiring CSF diversion, seizures, bone flap resorption, and reoperation. Functional outcome was assessed using the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) at six months. Kaplan-Meier analysis was used to evaluate complication-free survival, and multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression was performed to identify independent predictors of complications.
RESULTS: The cohort consisted of 184 patients with a mean age of 52.4 16.8 years; 64% were male. The most common indication for decompressive craniectomy was traumatic brain injury (55%), followed by ischemic stroke (42%) and intracerebral hemorrhage (2%). Early cranioplasty was performed in 37% of patients, intermediate in 34%, and delayed in 29%, with a median interval of 121 days between DC and CP. Autologous bone flap reimplantation was used in 86% of cases, whereas 14% received patient-specific synthetic implants. The overall postoperative complication rate was 26.6%. The most frequent complications were surgical site infection (13.0%), postoperative hematoma (8.2%), hydrocephalus (1.6%), and implant-related complications (3.8%). Complication rates did not significantly differ among timing groups (early 28%, intermediate 25%, delayed 26%; p = 0.61). Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated similar complication-free survival across groups (p = 0.64). Multivariate analysis identified higher comorbidity burden (CCI ≥4) as an independent predictor of postoperative complications (HR 2.1; 95% CI 1.2-3.7; p = 0.02), whereas timing of cranioplasty, cranial defect size, and implant material were not significant predictors.
CONCLUSIONS: Cranioplasty after decompressive craniectomy is generally safe, with complication rates comparable to those reported in the literature. In this cohort, the timing of cranioplasty did not independently influence postoperative complication rates. Instead, patient-related factors, particularly comorbidity burden, played a more significant role in determining outcomes. These findings support an individualized approach to cranioplasty timing based on patient condition and clinical factors rather than rigid temporal thresholds.

papers.title: [AI-manipulated medical records as part of medical child abuse].
papers.abstract: This case report describes a rare case of Medical Child Abuse (MCA) where AI-manipulated videos were used to fabricate seizures. A two-year-old boy was admitted to a pediatric emergency department under suspicion of epilepsy after his mother reported frequent seizures. During a five-day hospitalisation, the mother described two daily seizures, only witnessed by her. To substantiate the seizures, she presented three videos. Normal clinical findings and suspicious video footage led to concerns of MCA. When confronted, the mother admitted using generative AI tools to create the videos.

papers.title: ICFinder: ion channel identification and ion permeation residue prediction using protein language models.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ion channel dysfunction underlies many diseases (e.g., arrhythmias, epilepsy, cystic fibrosis), and uncharacterized channels may also contribute to pathology. Identifying such channels and their residues directly contacting the permeation pathway (i.e., ion permeation residues) is key to elucidating transport mechanisms and developing targeted therapies.
RESULTS: We developed BLAPE and CLAPE frameworks using the protein language model ESM-2 and curated datasets for high-throughput ion channel identification and permeation residue prediction. Our models achieved competitive performance, with relative improvements of 78% in Matthews correlation coefficients (MCC) on the ICIdentification dataset and 59% on the ICPermeation dataset compared with existing methods. Analysis of amino acid composition revealed enrichment for hydrophobic residues among ion permeation sites. Case studies on four diverse ion channels highlighted that CLAPE generally performs better than existing predictors and remains applicable to proteins lacking experimental structures, while also complementing structure-based pipelines such as AlphaFold3. We further applied our models to UniRef50 to predict potential ion channels, and made these results publicly available through the ICFinder webserver ( https://tianlab-tsinghua.cn/icfinder/ ), providing a ready-to-use resource for the research community. All source code is available at https://github.com/JueWangTHU/ICFinder .
CONCLUSIONS: BLAPE and CLAPE achieve competitive performance in ion channel identification and permeation residue prediction. ICFinder provides a practical resource for discovering potential ion channels, guiding target identification, and supporting drug design.

papers.title: Postoperative hemispheric hyperperfusion and status epilepticus after chronic subdural hematoma evacuation: a case report.
papers.abstract: Cerebral hyperperfusion syndrome (CHS) is rarely reported after chronic subdural hematoma (CSDH) evacuation. We describe a 40-year-old man who developed right hemispheric swelling, neurological deterioration, generalized seizures, and ipsilateral hyperperfusion on computed tomography perfusion after burr-hole drainage of a right CSDH. The overall clinical and radiological course was most consistent with probable CHS complicated by refractory status epilepticus, although seizure-related ictal or postictal hyperperfusion could not be fully excluded. He required strict blood pressure control, antiseizure therapy, deep intravenous anesthesia, and continuous electroencephalographic monitoring. Serial perfusion imaging showed gradual resolution of the hyperperfusion. He was discharged without neurological deficits and had returned to work with a modified Rankin Scale score of 0 by postoperative day 45. At 1 year, he remained seizure-free after withdrawal of all antiseizure medications, and an outside-hospital 24-hour ambulatory electroencephalography report showed no epileptiform abnormalities.

papers.title: The prevalence of dementia and cognitive impairment in patients with neurocysticercosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Neurocysticercosis (NCC) is a leading parasitic infection of the central nervous system and an important cause of neurological morbidity in endemic regions. Although seizures are well-characterized manifestations, the burden of cognitive impairment and dementia in NCC remains poorly quantified. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to estimate the prevalence of cognitive impairment and dementia among patients with NCC and to explore sources of between-study variability.
METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar (June-July 2025) and registered the protocol in PROSPERO (CRD420251106614). Observational studies reporting dementia or cognitive impairment in imaging-confirmed NCC were eligible. Data extraction and quality assessment were independently performed, and risk of bias was evaluated using the Hoy tool. Pooled prevalence estimates were generated using random-effects models with REML and Hartung-Knapp adjustments. Exact binomial (Clopper-Pearson) confidence intervals and logit-transformations were applied. Prespecified subgroup, meta-regression, and sensitivity analyses assessed heterogeneity.
RESULTS: Nine studies met inclusion criteria (N = 798 for cognitive impairment; N = 296 for dementia). The pooled prevalence of cognitive impairment was 50% (95% CI: 0.23-0.76; I²=97.87%) and dementia 10% (95% CI: 0.05-0.15; I²=49.11%). Subgroup analyses showed significant regional variation, with highest cognitive impairment prevalence in South America (68%). Cognitive assessment method did not account for heterogeneity. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of pooled estimates, and no significant small-study effects were detected.
CONCLUSION: Cognitive impairment affects approximately half of patients with NCC, while one in ten develop dementia. Geographic context and methodological factors largely drive between-study variability. These findings underscore NCC as an important contributor to neurocognitive morbidity in endemic regions and highlight the need for standardized cognitive assessment, harmonized diagnostic criteria, and longitudinal studies to clarify disease mechanisms and progression.

papers.title: Effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of epilepsy surgery in patients with refractory epilepsy: A systematic review of decision-analytic models.
papers.abstract: Our objective was to evaluate the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of epilepsy surgery for the treatment of patients with DRE. We carried out a systematic review of Decision Analytic Models (DAMs) in the main international databases regarding the comparison between epilepsy surgery versus medical treatment. We evaluated the relevance and credibility of the DAMs with the ISPOR-AMCP-NPC tool. We synthesized the results qualitatively. The certainty of the body of evidence was determined using the GRADE approach proposed for modeling studies. Clinical and economic outcomes were synthesized narratively because substantial heterogeneity existed across studies in epilepsy etiology, patient populations, model structures, perspectives, time horizons, and outcome definitions, precluding formal meta-analysis and quantitative pooling of cost-effectiveness estimates. Surgery was associated with higher reported rates of seizure freedom and seizure reduction than medical treatment, with seizure freedom ranging from 37.1% to 64.0% and seizure reduction from 24.6% to 42.2%. Reported QALY gains ranged from 0.3 to 3.0. Incremental costs varied substantially, ranging from savings of I$116,642 to additional costs of I$227,146 per patient. ICERs ranged from dominant (less costly and more effective) to I$291,091 per QALY gained. For seizure-related outcomes, ICERs ranged from I$454 to I$1,268 per 1% increase in seizure reduction and from I$5.83 to I$1,782 per 1% increase in seizure freedom, reflecting substantial variation in healthcare settings, perspectives, time horizons, and economic models. Epilepsy surgery is considered an effective and cost-effective option in patients with DRE, although the evidence is still low and very low certainty. So future studies of higher methodological quality are needed to better assess the picture and corroborate these results.Clinical trial number: Not applicable.

papers.title: Status epilepticus in mTORopathies: a systematic review of clinical features, management, and outcomes.
papers.journal: Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway plays a critical role in epileptogenesis; however, its involvement in human status epilepticus (SE) remains poorly understood. mTORopathies, genetic disorders defined by mutations that disrupt mTOR signaling, frequently manifest severe neurological complications, among which SE is particularly consequential.
METHODS: A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science was conducted for studies on mTORopathies and SE. We analyzed the clinical presentation, treatment strategies, and outcomes of all cases.
RESULTS: Eight hundred ninety-seven records were initially identified, of which 31 were included in this review. SE may manifest in different mTORopathies. SE often presents early, recurs frequently, and can be catastrophic. Refractory SE (RSE) predominantly affects neonates and infants and frequently occurs in the context of MCD. SE can be terminated with multiple anti-seizure medications (ASMs), alone or in combination with mTOR inhibitors. However, managing RSE is challenging. Current treatment strategies include novel ASMs, anesthetics, mTOR inhibitors, the ketogenic diet, immunotherapy, epilepsy surgery, and neuromodulation. A multifaceted approach is preferred to achieve seizure control and to improve developmental outcomes.
CONCLUSIONS: SE remains a significant clinical challenge in patients with mTORopathies. mTOR signaling may contribute to the pathogenesis of SE and could represent a potential therapeutic target. Further investigation in large cohort studies is needed to clarify the role of mTOR signaling in SE and to evaluate the effects of mTOR inhibitors and immunotherapies on outcomes in patients with SE/RSE.

papers.title: Refractory ventricular tachyarrhythmia following a suicidal massive caffeine overdose: a case report and review of emergency management.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Caffeine is one of the most widely consumed psychoactive substances worldwide and is readily accessible in tablet formulations and caffeinated beverages. Although moderate caffeine intake is generally considered safe, massive acute ingestion can result in severe toxicity involving the central nervous and cardiovascular systems. Life-threatening manifestations include seizures, profound electrolyte disturbances, metabolic derangements, and malignant ventricular arrhythmias. Because caffeine has favorable dialyzable properties, including low molecular weight, low protein binding, and a relatively small volume of distribution, extracorporeal toxin removal may play a critical therapeutic role in severe intoxication refractory to conventional supportive and antiarrhythmic management.
CASE PRESENTATION: We report the case of a previously healthy 16-year-old Iranian adolescent girl who intentionally ingested 10.8 g of caffeine in a suicide attempt. Approximately two hours after ingestion, she presented with markedly reduced consciousness, agitation, generalized tremor, intermittent tonic/myoclonic seizure-like activity, sinus tachycardia (180-190 beats/min), hypokalemia (serum potassium 2.7 mEq/L), primary metabolic acidosis, significant rhabdomyolysis, and electrocardiographic abnormalities including mild QRS widening and QTc prolongation (~ 500 ms). Urine toxicology screening was positive for caffeine, supporting the diagnosis in conjunction with the clear ingestion history and subsequent patient confirmation. Despite early airway protection, gastrointestinal decontamination, electrolyte and acid-base correction, dual antiarrhythmic therapy with amiodarone and lidocaine, and repeated synchronized electrical cardioversion, she developed recurrent refractory sustained ventricular tachycardia, transient progression to asystole requiring cardiopulmonary resuscitation, and persistent severe metabolic instability. Emergency intermittent hemodialysis was initiated approximately 3-4 h after emergency department arrival, resulting in rapid correction of metabolic acidosis, complete cessation of malignant ventricular arrhythmias, and sustained restoration of stable sinus rhythm. The patient subsequently demonstrated progressive neurological recovery without persistent cardiac or neurological sequelae.
CONCLUSION: This case highlights the potentially catastrophic cardiovascular consequences of massive caffeine intoxication and emphasizes the importance of early recognition, aggressive supportive care, rapid correction of metabolic abnormalities, and timely escalation to extracorporeal toxin removal in refractory cases. In patients with persistent malignant ventricular arrhythmias despite optimized pharmacologic and electrical management, intermittent hemodialysis may represent a life-saving therapeutic intervention capable of rapidly reversing toxicity and improving clinical outcomes.

papers.title: Nursing care for a patient with a twin pregnancy with complete hydatidiform mole and a coexisting fetus: a case report.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: A twin pregnancy with a complete hydatidiform mole and a coexisting fetus is a rare and high-risk pregnancy that occurs in 1/22,000 to 100,000 pregnancies, the risk of which may increase as a result of ovulation induction and assisted fertility techniques. These pregnant women are prone to sudden heavy bleeding, heart failure, and seizures during labor. Most of the patients choose to terminate their pregnancies after diagnosis. The best way in which to standardize clinical and nursing management for pregnant women who choose to continue their pregnancy is debatable.
CASE PRESENTATION: This is a report of a patient with lung metastasis after thyroid cancer surgery who underwent intrauterine insemination after administration of human menopausal gonadotrophin (HMG) to promote ovulation.After further counseling regarding maternal risks, the patient elected to continue the pregnancy, and the fetal heartbeat disappeared at 22+ 5 weeks of gestation. Through multidisciplinary treatment and specialized nursing care, maternal stabilization and preservation of future fertility potential were achieved.
CONCLUSION: This report describes the clinical management of a twin pregnancy with complete hydatidiform mole and a coexisting fetus (CHM&CF).This report explores the nursing experience associated with this rare condition. It thus provides a reasoned and effective framework to guide nursing practice in comparable clinical scenarios.

papers.title: Toll-Like Receptor-Driven Neuroinflammation in Neurological Disorders: Signaling Crosstalk and Therapeutic Opportunities.
papers.abstract: Toll-like receptors (TLRs) serve as pivotal mediators bridging innate immunity and neuroinflammation, orchestrating pathological cascades that drive neurological disorders. Beyond their sentinel role in pathogen recognition, aberrant TLR activation triggers intricate and destructive signaling networks, including activation of NF-κB, MAPK, JAK/STAT, and PI3K/AKT, alongside IRFs and type I interferon responses that converge on chronic neuroinflammation and subsequent neuronal damage. This review dissects TLRs' multilayered contribution to neuropathology, emphasizing their regulation of secondary inflammatory mechanisms, including NLRP3 inflammasome priming and activation, mTOR-driven metabolic dysregulation, SOCS-mediated feedback inhibition, inflammasome activation, and pyroptotic cell death. Critically, these signaling pathways create a pathological intersection with oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, amplifying a self-perpetuating cycle of neuronal injury that underlies conditions like Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), Huntington's disease (HD), and Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), Stroke, Multiple sclerosis (MS), Epilepsy and Traumatic brain injury (TBI). Against this neuropathological landscape, this review systematically evaluates emerging therapeutic strategies targeting TLR-mediated neuroinflammation, encompassing small molecule TLR antagonists, intracellular adaptor protein inhibitors targeting myeloid differentiation primary response 88 (MyD88) and TIR-domain-containing adapter-inducing interferon-β (TRIF), biologic therapies including monoclonal antibodies and fusion proteins, natural phytochemicals and nutraceuticals, Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-based genomic interventions, and cell-based immunomodulatory therapies, collectively representing a mechanistically diverse arsenal aimed at recalibrating the dysregulated innate immune response to achieve durable neuroprotection across the full spectrum of TLR-mediated neurological disorders.

papers.title: Adult Care in a Pediatric Hospital: Patterns and Implications of an Internal Medicine Consult Service at a Children's Hospital.
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Adults with childhood-onset conditions are increasingly admitted to children's hospitals, yet many pediatric systems lack the infrastructure and expertise to manage adult-related medical needs. One approach to bridge this gap is the use of an adult medicine consult service. We aim to describe the demographics, clinical complexity, and consultation patterns of patients admitted to a freestanding children's hospital and evaluated by an adult medicine consult service, which is a current gap in the literature.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: A retrospective descriptive cohort study was performed of admitted patients with a Hospital Medicine Adult Care (HMAC) service consult from July 2014 through June 2023.
RESULTS: Annual adult admissions increased over the study period, from 7.4% to 10.2% of all admissions. HMAC consulted on 1666 admissions for 1008 unique patients (median age, 27 years [range, 14-71 years]). The most frequent reasons for consult were venous thromboembolism prophylaxis (33.7%), age older than 25 years (21.2%), transition of care (7.6%), and hypertension (7.6%). HMAC physicians addressed a mean of 5.5 diagnoses per encounter. Patients averaged 3.6 admissions (range, 1-22) and 4.9 comorbidities (range, 0-21) each. The most common comorbidities were technology dependence (47%), solid tumor malignancy (22.5%), genetic conditions (20.2%), epilepsy (19.7%), congenital heart disease (17.4%), and cerebral palsy (15.7%).
CONCLUSIONS: Adult consult services in children's hospitals support a medically complex population with diverse childhood-onset and adult conditions and function as longitudinal clinical partners. These findings support the role of adult medicine expertise in children's hospitals to help recognize and manage adult-specific care needs and transitions.

papers.title: Symptom Impact in Angelman Syndrome: Results from the Hope in Action Caregiver Survey.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Angelman syndrome is a rare neurological disorder with no approved disease-modifying therapies. First-generation treatments are expected to be disease modifying but not curative, highlighting the importance of understanding symptoms with the greatest impact on individuals with Angelman syndrome and their caregivers to support patient-focused drug development. The Hope in Action survey was designed to capture lived experiences and inform an externally led, patient-focused drug development meeting.
METHODS: A global online survey was conducted among primary caregivers of individuals with Angelman syndrome. The survey was developed by a multidisciplinary team with input from advocates, caregivers, and representatives of the US Food and Drug Administration. Caregivers ranked top-3 domains and rated related symptoms affecting individuals with Angelman syndrome and those impacting caregivers; and top-5 priority symptoms to address with a new non-curative therapeutic. Analyses were descriptive.
RESULTS: When ranking and rating from lists of high-impact domains and symptoms, 370 caregiver participants most frequently identified communication, daily living skills, gross motor function, and cognition as impactful to individuals living with Angelman syndrome, and patients' independence and communication challenges as impactful to their own caregiver functioning, social participation, and mental health. Priority symptoms to treat with a new therapy included expressive communication, seizures, mobility, sleep, toileting, aggression, balance, and sustained attention/engagement.
CONCLUSIONS: Through the largest caregiver-reported study on Angelman syndrome symptom impact, we demonstrate an unmet treatment need and a profound impact on individuals and caregivers across a multitude of domains. These findings directly inform patient-focused drug development and reflect alignment of caregiver priorities and outcome measure selection for trials.

papers.title: Expression of nuclear factor kappa B-associated long non-coding RNAs in drug-naïve and valproic acid-treated epilepsy patients.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Epilepsy has a complex etiopathogenesis and frequently shows resistance to conventional antiseizure medications, underscoring the need for a deeper mechanistic understanding of the disease. Accumulating evidence implicates NF-κB-mediated neuroinflammation in epileptogenesis, and several long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are known to regulate this pathway. However, the expression patterns of the NF-κB-associated lncRNAs UCA1, ANRIL, and NKILA in epilepsy, and whether antiseizure medications can modulate them, remain largely unknown. This study therefore assessed these lncRNAs, together with the inflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-6, in drug-naïve and valproic acid (VPA)-treated epileptic patients compared with healthy controls.
METHODS: In a prospective, multicenter study with 120 adults, participants were divided into three groups: drug-naïve patients, VPA-treated patients, and healthy volunteers. Early morning blood samples were collected to measure serum levels of the selected lncRNAs and cytokines. Correlations between molecular markers and seizure parameters were examined.
RESULTS: Serum IL-1β, IL-6, UCA1, and ANRIL were significantly higher in drug-naïve patients than in healthy controls (p < 0.001, p < 0.001, p = 0.003, and p = 0.014, respectively), whereas NKILA showed no significant difference (p = 0.484). Compared with drug-naïve patients, VPA-treated patients showed no significant difference in IL-1β (p = 0.056) or IL-6 (p = 1.00); in the age- and sex-adjusted Bayesian model, UCA1 was significantly lower in the VPA group compared to the drug-naive group (p = 0.015) and no longer differed from controls (p = 0.424), whereas ANRIL remained largely unchanged. Serum IL-1β had a significant positive correlation with IL-6 (ρ = 0.58, p < 0.001) and ANRIL (ρ = 0.20, p = 0.028), and in drug-naïve patients seizure severity significantly correlate positively with UCA1 (ρ = 0.41, p = 0.009). On ROC analysis, IL-1β and IL-6 best discriminated untreated patients from controls (AUC = 0.84 and 0.96, respectively). These findings indicate heightened systemic inflammation in untreated epilepsy and support IL-1β and IL-6 as potential candidate biomarkers, with UCA1 as a potentially treatment-responsive lncRNA.
CONCLUSION: Our results identify serum UCA1 as the most notably altered lncRNA, significantly elevated in untreated epilepsy and potentially responsive to valproic acid. While IL-1β and IL-6 reflected the accompanying inflammation. These findings warrant further validation as candidate biomarker.

papers.title: Cesarean Myomectomy for Refractory Uterine Atony in an Eclamptic Woman with Multiple Fibroids: A Case Report from the Democratic Republic of Congo.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cesarean myomectomy remains a controversial procedure because of concerns regarding severe hemorrhage and peripartum hysterectomy. Recent reports suggest that it may be performed safely in carefully selected patients; however, the certainty of the available evidence remains very low, and reports describing its use for refractory uterine atony in women with eclampsia are scarce.
CASE PRESENTATION: We report the case of a 38-year-old Congolese woman, gravida 3 para 0 abortus 2, admitted to the University Clinics of Lubumbashi with generalized tonic-clonic seizures, severe hypertension (180/120 mmHg), and marked proteinuria, leading to a diagnosis of eclampsia. No ultrasound examination was performed before surgery because of the maternal emergency. After stabilization with magnesium sulfate and nicardipine, an emergency cesarean section was performed. A live female infant weighing 2030 g was delivered but died 30 minutes after birth in the neonatal intensive care unit.
OPERATIVE FINDINGS AND MANAGEMENT: Extensive uterine fibromyomatosis was identified, including nine fibroids, the largest measuring 16 × 10 × 8 cm and weighing approximately 1050 g. After hysterorrhaphy, severe uterine atony persisted despite uterine massage and oxytocin administration. Considering the patient's nulliparity and the wish to preserve the uterus, a conservative cesarean myomectomy was undertaken. Five major fibroids were removed, including the giant lower-segment fibroid. Progressive restoration of uterine tone was observed after myomectomy, with satisfactory hemostasis. Estimated blood loss was 900 mL, and total operative time was 90 minutes. Postoperatively, the patient received blood transfusion and recovered without complications. She was discharged in stable condition on postoperative day five.
CONCLUSION: In this patient, removal of the dominant fibroids was temporally associated with restoration of uterine tone and allowed emergency hysterectomy to be avoided. This single observation does not establish the safety or efficacy of the procedure, but suggests that cesarean myomectomy may be considered as a uterus-preserving option in carefully selected patients with refractory uterine atony related to extensive fibromyomatosis, provided that surgical expertise and blood transfusion capacity are available.

papers.title: Scalp Acupuncture Facilitating Blood Pressure Control in Pediatric Hypertensive Encephalopathy: A Case Report.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hypertensive encephalopathy (HE) in pediatric patients is a life-threatening condition requiring prompt and controlled blood pressure reduction to prevent neurological complications.
CASE ILLUSTRATION: We report a 7-year-old child with chronic kidney disease on continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis who presented with HE complicated by seizures and persistent hypertension despite intravenous nicardipine and multiple oral antihypertensive agents. Adjunctive manual scalp acupuncture was initiated using GV20 (Baihui), EX-HN1 (Sishencong), and additional ashi points.
RESULTS: Following treatment, the patient demonstrated a progressive reduction in blood pressure over seven sessions, accompanied by resolution of seizures, improvement in sleep, and reduction of associated symptoms such as neck pain. This improvement enabled gradual de-escalation of intravenous nicardipine and transition to oral therapy. No recurrent neurological events were observed during hospitalization or follow-up.
DISCUSSION: The observed clinical response suggests that scalp acupuncture may have a potential adjunctive role in pediatric HE. Plausible mechanisms include autonomic modulation, attenuation of sympathetic activity, improvement of cerebral blood flow and vascular reactivity, modulation of nitric oxide-related pathways, and neuroprotective or anti-inflammatory effects.
CONCLUSIONS: The application of scalp acupuncture for pediatric HE may be a promising therapeutic adjuvant in controlling blood pressure. Nevertheless, causality cannot be established from a single case, particularly given concurrent antihypertensive therapy and dialysis-based volume management. Further studies are needed to evaluate its efficacy and safety in this setting.

papers.title: Beyond Seizure Control: Building the Infrastructure for Disease-Modifying Therapies in Epilepsy.
papers.abstract: Rapid advances in disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) for epilepsy, including gene-based therapies, antisense oligonucleotides, and stem cell-derived approaches, are reshaping the treatment landscape. As these therapies move through clinical trials and toward regulatory review, they introduce complex clinical, operational, ethical, and equity considerations that extend well beyond traditional antiseizure medication management. Successful integration will require careful attention to patient selection, genetic and biomarker testing, multidisciplinary care models, infrastructure readiness, referral pathways, long-term safety monitoring, informed consent for novel and potentially irreversible interventions, access to clinical trials, and cost and reimbursement challenges. Significant investments in personnel, systems, and facilities may be necessary, raising important questions about implementation across diverse practice settings and the risk of widening disparities in care. Here, we review the evolving therapeutic pipeline and outline key considerations for safe, ethical, and equitable implementation.

papers.title: Impact of PPAR agonists on seizure suppression to disease modification using status-epilepticus experimental model: Role of the PPAR in metabolic-inflammatory pathway.
papers.abstract:
PURPOSE: This study explored the potential of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (α/γ) (PPAR modulators) for seizure control and the consequences of status epilepticus (SE) due to their anti-inflammatory and neuro-modulatory properties.
METHOD: A lithium-pilocarpine-induced status epilepticus (SE) model in Wistar rats determined the optimal dose of PPAR modulators (fenofibrate, pemafibrate, and saroglitazar) for seizure suppression. Based on seizure parameters, an efficacy study examined PPAR modulators alone and in combination with ASMs (valproate and perampanel). Evaluations of disease-modifying effects included neurobehavioral tests, electron microscopy for neurodegeneration, immunohistochemistry (NeuN for neuronal viability and GFAP for astrocytosis), Western blotting for PPARα, HMGCS2, NLRP3, and mTOR, and ELISA for antioxidant capacity and neuroinflammatory biomarkers.
RESULTS: The optimal doses of fenofibrate, pemafibrate, and saroglitazar were 200, 1.5, and 3 mg/kg, respectively. Compared with the SE-control group, drug-treated groups had higher latency (p<0.001), a lower number and percentage of rats with stage 3-4 seizures (p=0.003, for both), better memory retention (p=0.001), less myelin-sheath/axonal damage (p<0.001), significant differences in protein expressions [NeuN, PPARα, HMGCS2, mTOR, and NLRP3 (p<0.001)], and less neuroinflammation. The PPAR modulators + perampanel group had no stage 3-4 seizures. Compared to valproate alone, fenofibrate+valproate exhibited less neurodegeneration and astrocytosis in the hippocampus and cerebral cortex (p<0.001, for all). All PPAR modulator combinations with ASM groups had significantly higher PPARα and HMGCS2 expression.
CONCLUSION: PPAR modulators fenofibrate, pemafibrate, and saroglitazar have similar seizure-control potential. In the SE model, PPAR modulators with ASM showed significant neuroprotection and increased PPARα expression compared to ASM alone.

papers.title: Dopamine D2 receptor signaling alleviates seizure-related neuronal ferroptosis via MARCH8-mediated P2RX7 ubiquitination.
papers.abstract: Epilepsy affects over 70 million people worldwide and remains a major cause of morbidity and premature death. Although dopaminergic signaling dysfunction has been implicated in this disorder, its protective mechanisms are not fully understood. Here, we demonstrated that dopamine D2 receptor (D2R) expression is downregulated during seizures and that D2R signaling protects against seizure. We identified the purinergic receptor P2RX7- a known mediator of neuronal injury - as a downstream target of D2R. Activation of D2R signaling alleviated P2RX7-dependent neuronal ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of cell death, and attenuated seizure-related neuronal injury by promoting ubiquitination and degradation of P2RX7. Mechanistically, D2R signaling upregulated the E3 ubiquitin ligase MARCH8 in an AMPK-dependent manner. MARCH8 promoted K48-linked polyubiquitination of P2RX7, thereby targeting it for proteasomal degradation in neurons. The protective effect of D2R was attenuated in March8 knockout mice, supporting the involvement of MARCH8 in this pathway. Together, our findings identify a neuroprotective mechanism wherein D2R signaling promotes MARCH8-mediated ubiquitination and degradation of P2RX7, alleviating seizure-related neuronal ferroptosis. This work provides new insights into the pathogenesis of seizure-related neuronal injury and identifies potential therapeutic targets.

papers.title: EEG microstate alterations and their association with cognitive performance in late-onset epilepsy of unknown etiology: Comparison with Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cognitive impairment is common in late-onset epilepsy of unknown etiology (LOEU), but its electrophysiological correlates and relationship to Alzheimer's disease (AD) remain unclear. We compared resting-state electroencephalogram (EEG) microstate dynamics among LOEU, AD, and cognitively normal (CN) groups and examined their associations with cognitive performance.
METHODS: Eyes-closed 32-channel resting-state EEG recordings were analyzed from 60 patients with LOEU, 65 with AD, and 60 CN participants. Four canonical microstate classes (A-D) were identified. Group differences in microstate parameters were tested with false discovery rate correction. Associations with Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores were examined using multivariable interaction models adjusted for age, sex, education, and cerebral small vessel disease burden.
RESULTS: Microstate B duration was longer in LOEU and AD than in CN (Holm-adjusted p = 0.011 and 0.016), whereas microstate C occurrence was lower in both patient groups (p = 0.001 and 0.018). Microstate D duration was longer in LOEU than in CN and AD (both p = 0.038). For microstate A duration, the group interaction survived false discovery rate correction for MMSE (q = 0.0255) but not MoCA (q = 0.122). In LOEU, longer microstate A duration was associated with lower MoCA and MMSE scores. Pairwise slope comparisons were more negative in LOEU than in CN for both outcomes, whereas LOEU-AD slope differences were not significant.
CONCLUSIONS: LOEU showed altered resting-state EEG microstate dynamics that partly overlapped with those observed in AD, alongside a group difference in microstate D duration. Microstate A duration was associated with cognitive performance in LOEU, although this association did not significantly differ from that observed in AD. These findings support further investigation of EEG microstates as electrophysiological correlates of cognitive dysfunction in LOEU while also highlighting overlap with AD.

papers.title: Mechanisms and Functional Outcomes of Astrocytic Ca2+ Signaling.
papers.abstract: Astrocytic calcium (Ca2+) signaling is a central regulator of brain function, enabling astrocytes to integrate neuronal, vascular, and metabolic information across multiple spatial and temporal scales. Rather than passive support cells, astrocytes generate dynamic Ca2+ signals ranging from localized microdomain transients in perisynaptic processes to propagating intercellular waves. These signals arise from coordinated activity of plasma membrane channels, ligand-gated and G protein-coupled receptors, and intracellular Ca2+ handling systems. Through these mechanisms, astrocytic Ca2+ dynamics regulate essential processes including gliotransmitter release, synaptic modulation and plasticity, neurovascular coupling, and metabolic support. This multiscale signaling framework positions astrocytes as active hubs within the tripartite synapse and neurovascular unit, shaping both local circuit activity and global brain states. Notably, distinct signaling modalities-particularly microdomain events-function as key computational units that enable astrocytes to decode synaptic inputs. Disruption of Ca2+ homeostasis transforms this system into a driver of pathology. Dysregulated signaling promotes astrogliosis, neuroinflammation, excitotoxicity, and impaired neurovascular and metabolic coupling, and is implicated across disorders including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, epilepsy, stroke, and chronic pain. In this review, we highlight key knowledge gaps, including how microdomain and global Ca2+ signals are integrated, how Ca2+ dynamics couple to astrocytic metabolism and gliotransmission, and how these processes are reorganized across physiological and disease states. Addressing these challenges will be essential for deciphering astrocytic signaling logic and identifying precise pharmacological targets.

papers.title: Potter-Optimized Multiscale Bayesian Gated Axial Quantized Attention Network for Robust Multichannel EEG-ECG-Based Seizure Prediction.
papers.abstract: Accurate seizure prediction from physiological signals remains challenging because electroencephalography (EEG)-ECG recordings contain substantial noise, nonlinear temporal patterns, inter-subject variability, and complex cross-modal dependencies. To address these challenges, this study proposes a Potter-Optimized Multiscale Bayesian Gated Axial Quantized Attention Network (PM-BGAQAN) for robust three-state seizure prediction using multichannel EEG-ECG signals. The framework first employs adaptive weighted mean filter (AWMF) to suppress physiological noise while preserving relevant signal characteristics, followed by Convolutional Swin-Transformer Network (CSTN) for hierarchical multiscale spatiotemporal feature extraction and multimodal EEG-ECG representation learning. Inclusion of Bayesian Asymmetric Quantized Neural Network (BAQNN) is followed next for uncertainty-aware quantized features, whereas multiscale gated axial reverse attention (MGARA) exploits the discriminatory power of multiscale temporal dependencies using gated axial attention. Finally, Potter Optimization Algorithm (POA) optimizes the network parameters to improve classification performance and convergence. The proposed framework is evaluated using the Siena Scalp EEG dataset with timestamp metadata and the SeizeIT2 EEG-ECG wearable dataset for classification of preictal, ictal, and interictal states. Experimental results demonstrate an overall classification accuracy of 99.86%, whereas subject-independent validation achieves 98.06% average accuracy across the evaluated datasets. Ablation analysis further confirms the contribution of the individual components to the integrated framework. The results indicate that PM-BGAQAN provides an effective multimodal representation-learning strategy for robust seizure-state prediction and establishes a basis for future real-time, wearable, and clinically validated seizure monitoring systems.

papers.title: Untargeted Plasma Metabolomics Reveals Metabolic Alterations Associated With Idiopathic Epilepsy in Dogs.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Canine idiopathic epilepsy (IE) is one of the most common chronic neurological disorders in dogs, however, its underlying pathophysiology remains incompletely understood.
OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to characterise plasma metabolomic alterations associated with canine IE at two clinical points using an untargeted metabolomic approach.
METHODS: Plasma samples were collected from nine client-owned healthy dogs (Normal), and nine dogs with idiopathic epilepsy evaluated at acute seizure state (Epilepsy_D0) and after a 14-day seizure-free interval following antiepileptic treatment (Epilepsy_D14). For metabolomic analysis, plasma from three dogs was pooled to generate three biological pools per condition. Untargeted plasma metabolomic profiling was performed using LC-QTOF-MS in positive ionisation mode.
RESULTS: A total of 491 metabolites were retained for downstream analysis. Exploratory heatmap and principal component analyses showed differences in overall metabolic patterns among three groups. Differential abundance analysis identified distinct metabolite changes across the pairwise comparison. Pathway enrichment analysis of the significantly altered metabolites using the study-specific metabolite set as a custom background did not identify any pathway reaching statistical significance. Six metabolites of interest, namely pyridoxal, methylimidazoleacetic acid, 2-methylbutyroylcarnitine, indolelactic acid, homocitrulline and DL-Normetanephrine, showed distinct abundance patterns across the study conditions.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings provide preliminary evidence of plasma metabolic alterations associated with canine IE and differences between the acute seizure state and the 14-day seizure-free interval. Given the pooled biological design and limited effective sample size, these findings should be considered exploratory and require validation in larger cohorts using individual biological samples.

papers.title: Reduced Cytokine Production in a CYFIP1-Mediated Model of Autism Spectrum Disorder.
papers.journal: Bulletin of experimental biology and medicine
papers.abstract: CYFIP1 (Cytoplasmic FMR1 Interacting Protein 1) is a key component of the regulatory complex controlling actin polymerization, which is critically important for neuronal morphogenesis, synapse formation, and the maintenance of synaptic plasticity. Reduced CYFIP1 gene expression is associated with autism spectrum disorder, schizophrenia, epilepsy, and developmental delay. Cyfip1 haploinsufficient (Cyfip1+/-) mice demonstrate not only behavioral deficiency, but also diminished production of cytokines, key regulators of the immune response. This CYFIP1-dependent imbalance of immune system regulators may result in an inadequate response to proinflammatory stimuli in patients with neuropsychiatric symptoms. This phenomenon should be taken into account when developing therapeutic strategies for these patients.
